title: Sable and the Winter
premise: Ansel Pemberton, a late-night radio host, begins taking calls from listeners who died the previous week, and their voices are unmistakably real. As the dead callers multiply, every mirror in Ansel's house begins reflecting the room one second late, and in that stolen second, a figure called the Count appears, tallying the living for a winter that means to take them. Ansel, who has spent a lifetime refusing to believe in anything unseen, must finally accept that their family's survival depends on a memory Ansel buried long ago: the winter their own mother was taken. The story ends with Ansel trading their place on the count for the family's, walking into the mirror a second behind themselves, while the radio keeps broadcasting to an audience of the dead who finally remember their names.
about_author: Ivo Villalobos is a former overnight radio operator from coastal Maine who spent eleven years manning dead-air shifts before turning to horror fiction. He writes in the hours before dawn and claims he still can't look at a paused television screen for long.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. During a routine overnight broadcast, Ansel takes a call from Marisol Vega, a devoted listener who died six days earlier, and recognizes the voice instantly. Ansel rationalizes it as a prank, but the call ends with Marisol whispering, 'You're next on the list.' The emotional beat is denial sharpened into dread.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. At home, Ansel notices the bathroom mirror lagging—a hand raised, a reflection raised a beat after. Ansel tests every mirror in the house with a metronome; all of them are one second behind. The beat is quiet, clinical terror as skepticism begins to crack.

chapters.title: The Family That Doesn't Look
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Ansel's spouse Dara and teenage son Theo have stopped looking at mirrors entirely, and won't say why. Theo admits he's been seeing 'someone counting' in the hallway mirror at night. The beat is familial estrangement—each member hiding fear to protect the others.

chapters.title: Caller Number Nine
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. More dead callers phone in, each describing the same figure—the Count—standing behind them in their final week. One caller, a childhood neighbor, says the Count 'starts with the ones who don't believe.' Ansel realizes the show is being used as a ledger. Beat: guilt and complicity.

chapters.title: What Dara Buried
chapters.summary: Dara's POV. Dara confesses she saw the lagging mirror a month ago and said nothing, hoping it would pass like her grandmother's stories said it would. She reveals her family's rule: never answer a voice that knows your middle name. Beat: relief and resentment in equal measure.

chapters.title: The Count's Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Ansel maps the dead callers on a wall chart and finds they all died within a mile of the radio tower, in descending order of belief. Theo's name appears on the chart in handwriting Ansel doesn't recognize. Beat: the horror becomes personal and mathematical.

chapters.title: Winter Comes Early
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo skips school and visits the town archive, finding a 1974 photograph of a radio studio with Ansel's mother at the microphone—and a figure in the glass behind her. The beat is a child's terrible discovery that his parent's past is the pattern repeating.

chapters.title: Mother's Last Broadcast
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Ansel finally recalls the suppressed memory: their mother, also a radio host, vanished the winter Ansel was nine, mid-broadcast, and the family covered it as an accident. The mirrors lagged then too. Beat: identity collapses as Ansel realizes they were built to repeat her.

chapters.title: Static Between Us
chapters.summary: Dara's POV. Dara tries to take Theo to her sister's in another state, but every road loops back to town, and the car radio plays Ansel's show no matter the station. Beat: claustrophobia—the family learns the town itself is inside the count.

chapters.title: The Second Behind
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. In the lagging second, Ansel speaks to the figure in the mirror and it answers: it is not a ghost but an auditor, and it counts 'the unremembered.' Ansel realizes the dead callers are forgotten people. Beat: a horrifying logic that almost makes sense.

chapters.title: Names in the Ledger
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo finds his grandmother's old broadcast logs, each page ending with a list of names, the last entry unfinished—ending with his own first initial. Beat: dread of inheritance, the past reaching forward through paper.

chapters.title: Believe Me Now
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. On air, Ansel breaks format and tells the listening town the truth about the mirrors and the count. Half the callers beg Ansel to stop; the other half are already dead and cheering. Beat: reckless catharsis, belief as a weapon and a wound.

chapters.title: The Town That Forgot
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs, braided. Neighbors begin forgetting each other's names; the diner waitress calls Dara 'ma'am' with a stranger's politeness. The unremembered are being harvested first. Beat: communal grief, belonging eroding in real time.

chapters.title: Marisol's Bargain
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Marisol calls one last time and offers a deal: she can hold the count open for three nights if Ansel broadcasts her name and story so the town remembers her. Beat: fragile alliance with the dead, hope with a deadline.

chapters.title: Three Nights
chapters.summary: Dara and Theo's alternating POV. The family works the radio in shifts, telling the stories of the forgotten dead while the mirrors fall further behind—two seconds, then three. Beat: exhausted devotion, the family finally working as one.

chapters.title: What the Mirror Keeps
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. The lag grows to five seconds, and in that gap Ansel sees the mirror-room: a winter studio where the forgotten dead wait, including their mother, still at the microphone, still broadcasting. Beat: longing and horror fused—the dead aren't suffering, they're waiting to be remembered.

chapters.title: The Auditor's Terms
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. The Count appears in the flesh at the station and states its terms: the count must be balanced by dawn—one who is willing, remembered by no one, and who chooses the winter. Ansel, estranged, self-erased, fits perfectly. Beat: cold clarity of sacrifice.

chapters.title: Say My Name
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo, refusing to lose another parent, hijacks the broadcast to tell Ansel's whole story—every flaw, every year, every name—making Ansel impossible to forget. Beat: fierce, angry love as defiance of erasure.

chapters.title: The Last Call
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Ansel takes one final call: their mother's voice, telling them she stayed so Ansel could leave, and that being remembered is not the same as being kept. Ansel chooses anyway. Beat: acceptance without surrender.

chapters.title: Ahead of the Count
chapters.summary: Dara's POV. At dawn the family drives out as the mirrors snap back to real time, Dara watching the rearview for a figure that never comes. The town wakes remembering names it lost. Beat: exhausted, disbelieving relief.

chapters.title: A Second Behind Myself
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Ansel steps through the studio mirror into the winter room to balance the count in their mother's place, taking the microphone beside her. The broadcast continues on both sides of the glass. Beat: sorrowful transcendence—belonging found on the other side of identity.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: Theo's POV, epilogue. Years later, Theo hosts the overnight show. Each winter's first frost, a caller with Ansel's voice asks how the family is, and Theo answers, keeping them remembered, keeping them real. Beat: bittersweet continuity—grief turned into ritual, memory turned into keeping.
